newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania fund sells stake in Azomures.
newsitem.headline: Romania fund sells stake in Azomures.

text.p: Romania's main privatisation agency the State Ownership Fund (FPS) said on Wednesday it had sold a majority 51 percent stake in listed Azomures SA fertiliser maker to a Romanian trading company.
But the market community was baffled by the way in which the FPS handled the sale, saying the deal lacked transparency.
"The FPS signed a contract on February 4 with Euro Trading Chemicals SRL, which is associated with Azomures employees, after analysing two bids for the stake," an FPS statement said.
The statement, released one day after the deal, denied a late Tuesday state television report saying the successful bidder was Turkish trading company Omnimpex Chemicals.

The FPS statement did not give an overall figure for the purchase by Euro Trading and did not say how many shares it had sold. It only said Euro Trading would have to pay in cash 3,600 lei per share over the next 90 days. Bourse data put Azomures' share capital at 172 billion lei.
Euro Trading officials could not be contacted.
The nominal value of an Azomures share was lowered to 1,000 lei from 25,000 after oversubscription in a mass selloff.
Under the contract, Euro Trading pledges to invest the equivalent of $38.7 million over five years and raise monthly net wages -- now at $100 -- to $300 by 2000, the FPS said.
The FPS said Omnimpex did not contest tender results.
The Bucharest bourse said it had learned of the FPS deal from media reports.

"Sale of a main stake in a listed stock must be announced as soon as a contract is signed," bourse manager Stere Farmache told Reuters, adding that FPS should have informed Azomures, with Azomures reporting the sale to the bourse in writing.
"So far, Azomures did not report the sale," he said.
"It was wrong for the FPS to be so opaque, especially when the sale involves a listed stock which trades extremely well," a Bucharest broker said.

Azomures, the only company to trade on the first tier, is seen as a highly liquid, financially solid stock. It has been an attraction since it joined the bourse last January, taking at least half the turnover of almost all sessions.

"The FPS sale should have gone through the bourse. I can understand the FPS wanted to attract an industrial rather than a speculative investor but shunning the exchange will have a negative impact on the market," a trader said.
"We expect a market price of around 1,500 lei after the split. And the FPS selling price is a lot higher," he said.
"What will happen is that the market price will get in line with the selling price and investors will pay a price boosted by book value rather than better company performance," he said. ($=5,978 lei)
